q: You are checking the pilotage plan your mate wrote for tonight's entry. What is the most useful thing to add to it?
a: What you will see at each turn and the danger past it
o: The opening hours of the marina office
The full tidal curve for the whole day
The latitude and longitude of every mark
why: A pilotage plan is what you expect to see, when, and what lies beyond if you miss it — not data to look up.

fig.title: Pilotage plan — Porto Vecchio
lines: 3  Pier head → turn to port for the marina

q: You are writing the pilotage plan card for tomorrow's entry. Why do you write every heading and bearing in degrees magnetic?
a: The helm's compass and the hand-bearing compass read magnetic
o: The compass rose on the chart shows magnetic only
Magnetic bearings are free of variation and deviation
The plotter can display magnetic bearings only
why: In the cockpit you steer and take bearings by magnetic compass — the card must need no arithmetic.

q: You are on leg 2 of your plan. When do you expect the turning mark abeam?
why: Use speed over the ground: 1.3 M ÷ 4.5 kn = 0.29 h = 17 min; 2140 + 17 min = 2157.

fig.title: Log — night entry
lines: Leg 2: 047°M, 1.3 M to the Fl G 3s

q: Your plan says the turning mark should be fine to starboard by now. What do you do?
a: Stop, fix your position and go back to the fairway buoy
o: Press on along the heading — it will show up soon
Turn to starboard and search for the green light
Speed up to get in before the night gets darker
why: A mark not seen when the plan expects it means you may not be where you think: stop, fix, return to the last safe point.

fig.title: Night entry
lines: 2215  Fairway buoy abeam; leg 2 is 1.0 M
Plan: Fl(2) G 6s fine to stbd by 2228

q: You are entering on the leading lights at night and see them like this. What do you do?
a: You are to port of the line: come to starboard
o: You are to starboard of the line: come to port
You are on the line: hold your heading
You are to port of the line: come further to port
why: Rear light open to the left of the front means you are left of the line — steer right until they are one above the other.

fig.note: Leading lights ahead · rear light open to the left

q: There are no leading marks into the bay, so you pick a natural transit to hold your line clear of the reef. Which pair do you choose?
a: A chapel high on the hill behind the end of the jetty
o: Two trees on the beach a few metres apart
A yacht at anchor in line with the beach bar
The end of the jetty in line with a moored boat
why: A good transit uses two fixed, easy-to-see objects far apart: the farther the rear from the front, the sooner it shows you are off.

q: You are entering on the charted leading line with the marks exactly in line, yet the plotter shows you here. What do you trust?
a: The transit — the plotter's chart may be offset
o: The plotter — GPS is good to a few metres
Neither — stop until the two agree again
The plotter — steer west to put it on the line
why: Marks in line put you on the line whatever the screen says; a plotter chart can be offset from GPS by tens of metres.

q: You are motoring in on the 045°M transit and keep the marks in line, but the compass shows 055°M. What does it mean?
a: A cross-stream sets you to port; holding the transit is right
o: A cross-stream sets you to starboard; steer 045°M
The compass has 10° of deviation; steer 045°M
The transit is wrong; steer by the compass instead
why: On a transit the heading is whatever keeps the marks in line: bow 10° to starboard of it means the stream sets you to port.

q: What does this line of your pilotage plan tell you?
a: The light must bear 125°T or less to keep clear
o: The light must bear 125°T or more to keep clear
Steer 125°T straight for the light on this leg
Pass the light no more than 1.25 M off
why: NMT = not more than: the clearing bearing is a limit, and the plan says which side of it is safe.

fig.title: Pilotage plan — leg 2
lines: (shoal lies on the far side of the line)

q: You are coasting east at night past the shoal, using the clearing bearing on the lighthouse. Your hand-bearing compass gives the light 084°M. What do you do?
a: Alter to starboard until it bears 080°M or less
o: Alter to port until it bears 080°M or less
Hold course — over 080°M is the safe side
Alter to port until it bears 090°M or more
why: The shoal lies where the light bears more than 080°M; heading east, moving south (to starboard) brings the bearing down.

q: You are heading north into the bay between two reefs. Where are you and what do you do?
a: 009°T — west of the safe corridor; come to starboard
o: 005°T — inside the corridor; hold your course
009°T — east of the safe corridor; come to port
007°T — inside the corridor; hold your course
why: 007°M + 2°E = 009°T, over the NMT 008°T limit: the church bears too far right, so you are west — move east.

q: You want a clearing line past a reef that runs parallel to your course. Which object makes the best one?
a: A fixed light near ahead, whose line clears the reef
o: A tower on the beam, whose bearing changes fastest
A ship at anchor ahead, lying on the right line
Any object at all — the plotter checks the line
why: A clearing line runs from a fixed, charted object past the danger's edge, roughly along your track — ahead or astern.

q: You leave harbour at night along the leading line, steering 040°M with the lights astern. What should they bear by hand-bearing compass?
why: A back bearing is the reciprocal: 040° + 180° = 220°.

fig.note: Looking astern · leading lights in line

q: Leaving the harbour on the planned track, you take a back bearing of the harbour light. Where are you and what do you do?
a: East of the line: alter to port
o: West of the line: alter to starboard
East of the line: alter to starboard
On the line: 5° is within the margin
why: Light astern at 205°M puts you on its 025° line, east of the 020° track — to starboard, so come to port.

fig.title: Leaving Ermoupoli
lines: Track 020°M away from the harbour light
Rocks 2 cables either side of the track

q: You are following the 10 m contour north at night, the land to starboard. Where are you and what do you do?
a: 6.8 m charted — inshore of it; alter to port
o: 9.6 m charted — on it; hold your course
8.2 m charted — inshore of it; alter to starboard
6.8 m charted — offshore of it; alter to starboard
why: Charted depth = sounding − height of tide: 8.2 − 1.4 = 6.8 m, shallower than 10 m, so you are inshore — head out.

q: You plan to follow a depth contour along this coast for a night approach. Which do you choose?
a: The 20 m line — clean, steep and with margin
o: The 5 m line — closest to the harbour mouth
The 2 m line — the sounder reads it most clearly
Any of them — every contour is equally good
why: A good handrail is a steep, even contour well outside the dangers, so the sounder shows at once when you cross it.

q: You are coasting east past an estuary mouth and this red can buoy lies ahead. Which side do you leave it?
a: To starboard — you are going against the buoyage
o: To port — you are going with the buoyage
To port — a red mark is always kept to port
Either side — it only marks the estuary
why: Lateral marks follow the charted direction of buoyage; heading against it (east, arrow west), red is left to starboard.

q: You are leaving harbour in the Caribbean (IALA region B) and see this buoy ahead. Which side do you leave it?
a: On your port side
o: On your starboard side
On either side, keeping well off
Close on your starboard side
why: Region B: red marks the starboard side going in ("red right returning"), so going out it stays to port.

fig.note: IALA region B · heading out to sea

q: Heading upstream with the buoyage, you want to stay in the main channel. How do you pass this mark?
a: Leave it to port; the main channel lies to starboard
o: Leave it to starboard; the main channel lies to port
Either side; both channels are the same
Leave it to port; the main channel lies to port
why: Region A: red with a green band, Fl(2+1) R, is a port-hand mark with the preferred channel to starboard.

fig.title: Mark at the fork
lines: IALA region A, going with the buoyage
Red can, one broad green band

q: The marina you are bound for lies up the minor branch of the river. Which side of the mark at the fork do you leave it?
a: Leave it to port, then follow the minor channel's marks
o: Leave it to starboard — green is kept to starboard
Leave it to starboard, then turn right behind it
Either side — it only marks the junction
why: Fl(2+1) G with a red band: preferred channel to port. The minor branch is on its other side, so the mark goes to port.

fig.title: River fork, IALA region A
lines: Green cone, broad red band, Fl(2+1) G

q: Coasting by day along a broken Croatian shore, you see this mark fine on the bow, between you and a group of islets. Where is the safe water?
a: East of the mark
o: West of the mark
North of the mark
South of the mark
why: East cardinal: black-yellow-black, cones point away from each other; the safe water is to its east.

fig.note: Fine on the bow, islets beyond

q: On watch at night you time an unlit mark's light ahead. What is it and how do you pass it?
a: A west cardinal: pass west of it
o: An east cardinal: pass east of it
A south cardinal: pass south of it
A west cardinal: pass east of it
why: Nine quick flashes every 15 s is Q(9) 15s — a west cardinal, like nine o'clock; the safe water is to its west.

fig.title: Night watch
lines: White light fine on the starboard bow
Quick flashes: counted nine, then dark

q: Your crew has drawn the night route on the plotter past this mark. What do you tell them?
a: Re-route east of it — it is an east cardinal
o: Fine — keep the mark close on your starboard side
Re-route north of it — it is a north cardinal
Fine — a cardinal may be passed on either side
why: Q(3) is an east cardinal, three o'clock: the danger lies west of it, where the route goes.

q: Your crew asks why this light adds a long flash after its quick flashes. What do you tell them?
a: So that six can't be miscounted as three or nine
o: To show that the danger lies to the north of it
To show that it marks a new, uncharted danger
To show that it is the last mark of the channel
why: South cardinal Q(6)+LFl: the long flash makes the group of six unmistakable next to the E (3) and W (9) marks.

fig.note: South cardinal

q: At night you identify this mark off a shoal and take its bearing: 200°M. Where are you?
a: North-north-east of it — on its safe side
o: South-south-west of it — on its danger side
North-north-east of it — on its danger side
South-south-west of it — on its safe side
why: It bears 200° from you, so you are on its 020° side; a north cardinal has its safe water to the north.

fig.note: Bearing from you 200°M

q: On watch you count an unbroken white light ahead. Which mark is it and where is its safe water?
a: The north cardinal: pass north of it
o: The east cardinal: pass east of it
The west cardinal: pass west of it
The north cardinal: pass south of it
why: Twenty flashes in 10 s is 120 a minute — very quick, unbroken: VQ, the north cardinal.

fig.title: Night watch
lines: White light ahead, flashing without a break
Chart nearby: N card VQ · E card VQ(3) 5s

q: Your route between two Ionian islands passes this mark, alone in open water. How do you pass it?
a: Either side, with a good berth — it sits on the danger
o: Close on either side — it marks safe water
Keep it to port — it is a lateral mark
Keep north of it — it is a north cardinal
why: Isolated danger mark: black with a red band, two balls, Fl(2) — navigable water all round, the danger under it.

fig.note: Alone in open water

q: Arriving at night off an unfamiliar harbour, your pilotage plan starts from this mark. What does it tell you?
a: Safe water all round — the landfall for the approach
o: A danger under it — pass at least a cable off
The port side of the channel — keep it to port
A restricted zone — do not pass inside it
why: Safe water mark: red and white stripes, red ball, Iso, Oc, LFl 10s or Mo(A) — a landfall or fairway mark.

fig.note: Start of the pilotage plan

q: Looking for an anchorage off a beach in July, you see a line of small yellow buoys about 150 m off it. What do you do?
a: Anchor outside the line — it marks a bathing zone
o: Anchor inside the line — it marks a quiet zone
Pass inside the line — yellow marks safe water
Keep north of each buoy — they are cardinals
why: Yellow special marks show a feature the chart or pilot book describes — here a bathing zone where craft may not go.

q: On passage at night you see this light. The mark is on no chart and in no notice you have. What do you do?
a: Keep well clear — it marks a new, uncharted wreck
o: Pass close — it marks the safe water
Ignore it until it appears on the chart
Keep it to port — it marks a channel
why: Emergency wreck marking buoy: blue and yellow stripes, yellow cross, Al Bu Y — laid on a new danger before notices catch up.

fig.note: Not on the chart

q: Entering at night, you see two red lights on the north side. Which one is the breakwater head?
a: The one lit most of the time, with two short eclipses
o: The one that flashes twice, then stays dark
The one that alternates red and white
The one that is lit 4 s and dark 4 s
why: Oc(2) = occulting in groups of two: light longer than dark, with two short eclipses in each 8 s.

fig.title: Pilot book — Limenas
lines: Tonight: two red lights on the N side

q: The inner harbour light is shown on the chart like this. What will you see when you time it?
a: Light for 2 s and dark for 2 s, over and over
o: A short flash every 4 s, dark in between
Light for 4 s with a short eclipse
Steady light, never dark at all
why: Iso = isophase: equal periods of light and dark; the period 4 s gives 2 s of each.

fig.note: Inner harbour light, ahead

q: Your bearing of the light on the islet holds steady, but its colour goes white–red–white–red. What does the change tell you?
a: Nothing about your position — it is an alternating light
o: You keep crossing a sector edge — alter away
The red marks a danger sector — turn back
The light is faulty — report it to the coastguard
why: Al WR shows white and red in turn on every bearing; a sector light changes colour only as your bearing changes.

fig.title: Night watch
lines: Light on the islet: bearing steady 295°M
Chart: Al WR 6s, no sectors shown

q: You are 9 M off this lighthouse tonight. Do you expect to see it?
a: Probably not — 16M assumes 10 M visibility
o: Yes — it shows 16 M in any visibility
Yes — a light 24 m high is seen from 24 M
Yes — lights are seen further at night
why: Nominal range is for a meteorological visibility of 10 M; in 2 M visibility the luminous range is far shorter.

q: Heading in on about 000°T towards the directional light, you see it red. What do you do?
a: You are west of the white sector: come to starboard
o: You are east of the white sector: come to port
You are west of the white sector: come to port
Red means danger ahead: stop and turn back
why: Red shows on bearings 004°–009°: the light bears east of north, so you lie west of the line — turn east.

q: Approaching on the directional light, you take its bearing. Which sector are you in and what do you do?
a: 130°T — in the white sector; hold your heading
o: 136°T — in the red sector; come to starboard
133°T — in the red sector; come to starboard
130°T — in the green sector; come to port
why: Sectors are true bearings from seaward: 133°M − 3°W = 130°T, inside the white 128.5°–131.5°.

q: Coasting west at night, you see the light on the point turn from white to red. What does it mean?
a: You have entered the sector over the shoal: get back into white
o: You are on the leading line into the harbour
It is an alternating light: ignore the colour
You are past the shoal: you can close the coast
why: A red sector of a coastal light covers a danger; seeing red means you are in it — move until the light is white again.

q: Entering a Greek harbour at night, you see the two breakwater lights. Where do you steer?
a: Between them, the red to port and the green to starboard
o: Between them, the red to starboard and the green to port
Outside the red light, keeping it to starboard
Outside the green light, keeping it to port
why: Region A harbour lights follow the lateral rule: red on the port side going in, green on the starboard side.

fig.note: Harbour entrance ahead · IALA region A

q: Approaching the road bridge at night, your crew points at the brightest arch, lit by street lamps. Which arch do you take?
a: The arch between the two green lights
o: The brightest arch, lit by the street lamps
Any arch between two red lights
The arch with the single white light
why: The pilot book gives the bridge's own lights: the navigable arch is the one between the green pair; red marks the piers.

fig.title: Pilot book — road bridge
lines: Navigable arch: F G on each side of it
Other arches: F R on the piers

q: Approaching the harbour entrance, you see this on the signal mast, as the pilot book describes. What do you do?
a: Hold off clear of the entrance and wait
o: Enter with care — it signals one-way traffic
Enter — the signal is for big ships only
Stop and anchor in the entrance itself
why: IALA port traffic signals: three fixed red lights, vertical — vessels shall not proceed.

fig.note: Signal mast at the entrance · steady lights

q: You are a mile off the port when the signal mast shows this. What does it mean?
a: A serious emergency: stop or divert as instructed
o: One-way traffic: enter with care
The port is closed for the night: anchor off
A ship is leaving: wait to starboard of it
why: IALA port traffic signals: three red lights flashing — serious emergency, all vessels stop or divert as instructed.

fig.note: Signal mast · all three flashing

q: Arriving at a busy commercial port, you see these lights on the signal mast. What do you do?
a: Enter only when port control tells you to
o: Enter — the signal means two-way traffic
Enter — the signal means one-way traffic
Stay out — the port is closed to yachts
why: IALA port traffic signals: green, white, green — a vessel may proceed only when she has specific orders to do so.

fig.note: Signal mast · steady lights

q: Arriving at night, you can't pick out the breakwater lights against the town. What do you do?
a: Stand off and time each light until both heads are certain
o: Head for the first red and green pair you see
Steer for the middle of the town lights
Go in fast before the confusion gets worse
why: Background lights hide harbour lights: stay in safe water, identify each by its characteristic, then commit.

fig.note: Town ahead · breakwaters: Fl R 5s, Fl G 5s

q: You are planning a night entry on the plotter and are about to put the turning waypoint on the buoy itself. Why don't you?
a: On autopilot it would steer you straight onto the buoy
o: The plotter can't store a waypoint on a mark
A waypoint on a buoy upsets the AIS display
Buoys are charted exactly, so it isn't needed
why: Put waypoints a safe distance off marks and hazards: a route to a buoy leads onto it, as it does for everyone else.

q: Feeling your way into a cove, you zoom right in on the plotter. What do you trust?
a: The pilot book — zooming in adds no detail
o: The plotter — it is zoomed to the finest detail
The plotter — electronic charts are always newer
Neither — you go by the echo sounder alone
why: Over-zoom only enlarges a small-scale survey; rocks too small for it are simply not there on the screen.

fig.title: Entering the cove
lines: Plotter: zoomed ×8, clear to the beach
Pilot book plan: rocks 50 m off the point

q: You decide to go into harbour rather than wait for the fog to lift. How do you set the boat up?
a: Slow speed, fog signal, lookout forward, radar and sounder watched
o: Cruising speed, to spend less time in the fog
Slow speed, crew below out of the way, autopilot on
Full speed on the plotter route, radar off to save power
why: In fog: safe speed, the sound signal, a lookout and every aid — radar, sounder, plotter — cross-checked.

fig.title: Fog
lines: 1 M from the entrance, radar on
Crew of four, all on deck

q: Fog closes in 3 M from the harbour. You have no radar. What is the safest way in?
a: Along the 20 m line to the fairway buoy, slow, then its bearing in
o: A straight line for the entrance at cruising speed
Anchor where you are, in 45 m of water
Follow a fishing boat that seems to know the way
why: Without radar use what you can check: a clean contour as a handrail to a known mark, then a short leg in from it.

q: Arriving at dusk at this harbour for the first time, what do you assume about the breakwater?
a: It may run further out than charted: give it a wide berth
o: The chart is right — it is the official document
The plotter is right — it shows the light where it is
The work was never finished — ignore the note
why: When sources disagree, plan for the worse case: the newest note may be right and the old chart out of date.

fig.title: Arriving at Kamari
lines: Your chart: older edition, no extension
Plotter: the light at the old head

q: You and one crew bring the boat into a strange harbour at night. How do you split the work?
a: One steers the headings called; the other navigates and calls the marks
o: Both watch the plotter while the autopilot steers
The skipper steers and navigates; the crew does fenders
The crew navigates from below; the skipper steers by eye
why: In pilotage one person steers and one navigates from the cockpit, calling headings and marks and checking each one.

q: Entering an unfamiliar harbour at night, your navigator stays at the chart table calling "turn now" from the plotter. Why is this a poor set-up?
a: Nobody on deck checks the marks against the plan
o: The plotter is less accurate below decks
The helm should be the one at the plotter
The skipper should be below instead
why: The navigator belongs in the cockpit with the plan, eyes on the marks; the plotter is a cross-check, not the pilot.

q: You are rounding a headland at night on radar, with a parallel index line set to pass it 0.6 M off. The echo looks like this. What do you do?
a: Alter to port — you would pass inside 0.6 M
o: Alter to starboard — you would pass outside 0.6 M
Hold on — the echo sits on the index line
Alter to starboard — you would pass inside 0.6 M
why: On track the echo slides down the index line; inside the line, your track passes closer than planned — turn away from it.

fig.note: Radar, north-up · plan: pass the headland 0.6 M off

q: Before you set a parallel index line, you check where your present COG takes you. How far off the headland will you pass?
why: Passing distance = range × sin(angle off the COG): 2.0 × sin(075° − 045°) = 2.0 × 0.5 = 1.0 M.

fig.title: Radar and plotter, 0120
lines: Plan: pass the headland 0.8 M off

q: Rounding a headland at night, you keep the coast outside a VRM ring, as your plan says. The echo now cuts inside the ring on the port bow. What do you do?
a: Alter to starboard until the echo is outside the ring
o: Alter to port to put the echo back on the ring
Hold on — the ring shows the rocks are past
Shorten the range scale and hold on
why: The VRM is a clearing range: coast inside the ring means you are closer than the safe distance — open it out.

fig.note: Plan: keep the coast outside 0.8 M · rocks 0.3 M off

q: Your radar is head-up and you want it to show the moment of the turn in your plan. Where do you set the EBL?
a: 290° relative — 70° on the port bow
o: 070° relative — 70° on the starboard bow
310° relative — 50° on the port bow
300° relative — 60° on the port bow
why: A head-up EBL reads relative to the bow: 300° − 010° = 290° relative, i.e. 70° to port.

fig.title: Radar — entering at night
lines: Plan: turn to 300°M for the entrance

q: You are writing a pilotage plan for a harbour you may have to enter in fog, using the radar. What do you add for each turn?
a: The range and bearing of a steep echo there
o: The colour and rhythm of each buoy's light
The VHF channel of the harbour office
The lat/long of each turn for the radar
why: In fog each turn needs a radar check: the range and bearing of a good echo, ready to set on the VRM and EBL.

q: Crossing at night, you see this on the radar. What does it tell you, and what do you do?
a: A new-wreck buoy's racon — keep well clear
o: A fairway buoy's racon — steer for it
A ship's radar beacon — ignore it
Interference — retune the gain and carry on
why: An emergency wreck marking buoy carries a racon coding Morse D: a new danger, not yet on the chart.

fig.title: Radar, crossing at night
lines: Echo 1.5 M ahead with a racon:

q: You are copying the entry line from the pilot book onto your pilotage card. What do you write?
why: Pilot books give true bearings from seaward: 048°T − 2°E = 046°M (east is least).

fig.title: Pilot book — Vathy
lines: in line with the mole head

q: You are timing your run inside the harbour from the pilot-book plan. How long will it take from the mole head to the fuel berth at the speed limit?
a: 9 min
o: 15 min
1½ min
6 min

fig.title: Pilot book plan — Kastela
lines: Mole head to the fuel berth: 4.5 cables
Speed limit in the harbour 3 kn

q: The pilot book's plan of tonight's harbour looks like this. Which line do you take through the entrance?
a: Favour the east side, clear of the W head's rocks
o: Hug the W head — the deep water is close in
Midway, then round the W head close in
Close to the W head, rocks to starboard
why: The plan shows rocks running out from the W head: keep to the side of the entrance away from them, in the charted depth.

q: You are 4 M off your planned harbour at dusk and check the pilot book. What do you do?
a: Divert to a harbour sheltered from the south
o: Run in fast on the back of a wave
Anchor off the entrance until it eases
Go in slowly down the middle of it
why: The pilot book's warning fits tonight's wind exactly: an entrance with breaking swell is no place to try — go elsewhere.

fig.title: Pilot book — Ag. Nikolaos
lines: S winds over F5: heavy swell breaks
across the entrance — do not enter

q: Approaching at night, you point the bow at the directional light and read the steering compass. Which sector are you in?
a: 128°T — the white
o: 130°T — the red
122°T — the green
132°T — the red
why: 127°C − 2°W deviation = 125°M; + 3°E variation = 128°T: inside the white, 124°–129°.

q: Motoring upstream with the buoyage at night, you see these lights on the bridge ahead. Where do you pass under it?
a: Under the white light, midway between red and green
o: Close by the red light, leaving it to starboard
Under the next span, away from the lights
Close by the green light, leaving it to port
why: Bridge marking: red and green lights mark the sides of the navigable span; a white light marks the centre of the channel.

fig.note: Road bridge ahead · heading upstream, region A

q: You are waiting at a lifting bridge whose signals follow the IALA port traffic signals. As the span lifts, it shows this. What do you do?
a: Go through — one-way traffic, your way
o: Go through, ready to meet boats coming the other way
Wait for orders on VHF, then go through
Hold off — the span is about to come down
why: IALA port traffic signals: three fixed green lights — vessels may proceed, one-way traffic.

fig.note: Lifting bridge · steady lights (IALA port signals)

q: At 2200 you reach the commercial port where you will spend the night, and its signal mast shows this. What does it allow?
a: Entry now — with two-way traffic in the entrance
o: Entry now — one-way traffic, your way only
Entry only once port control orders it
No entry — wait outside the port
why: IALA port traffic signals: green, green, white — vessels may proceed; two-way traffic.

fig.note: Port signal mast · steady lights

q: Your 12 m yacht can keep safely outside the dredged channel, as the pilot book allows small craft to. The signal mast shows this. What may you do?
a: Go in outside the main channel, keeping clear
o: Nothing — no vessel may move in the port
Go in down the main channel with care
Go in only once port control orders it
why: Three fixed red: do not proceed — but a yellow light beside the top one exempts vessels able to keep outside the main channel.

fig.note: Signal mast · steady lights

q: On your first charter in the Caribbean (IALA region B), you meet this mark off a reef. Where is its safe water?
a: East of it — cardinals are the same in A and B
o: West of it — region B reverses the cardinals
Either side — it stands on the reef itself
West of it — the topmarks point at the reef
why: Region B changes only the colours of lateral marks; cardinal marks are the same: an east cardinal has safe water to the east.

fig.note: IALA region B · Caribbean charter

q: Coming in from sea at night in IALA region B, you see this light ahead marking the channel. Which side do you leave it?
a: To starboard — red right returning
o: To port — red is the port side, as in Europe
Either side — it marks the channel's centre
To port — you are going with the buoyage
why: In region B red marks are starboard-hand when entering from sea: 'red right returning'.

fig.note: Entering from sea · IALA region B (Bahamas)

q: Your marina lies up the main channel. Which side of this mark at the fork do you leave it?
a: To port — the main channel lies to starboard
o: To starboard — the main channel lies to port
To starboard — green is the starboard-hand colour
Either side — both branches are main channels
why: In region B green is port-hand; a green can with a red band, Fl(2+1) G, marks the preferred channel to starboard.

fig.title: Region B · heading in from sea

q: Heading west towards your next waypoint, your stopwatch gives this for the light dead ahead. Which mark is it, and how do you pass it?
a: South cardinal — pass south, leaving it to starboard
o: South cardinal — pass north, leaving it to port
West cardinal — pass west, holding your course
North cardinal — pass north, leaving it to port
why: VQ(6)+LFl 10s is a south cardinal: safe water to the south — heading west, that leaves the mark to starboard.

fig.title: Night watch · heading 270°T
lines: Very quick flashes: six, then a long one
Your plan: pass north of the mark

q: Crossing between two islands at night, you time this light. What mark is it on?
a: An isolated danger mark
o: A safe water mark
A south cardinal mark
A preferred channel mark
why: A white Fl(2) is the isolated danger light: the danger is right under the mark — pass with a good berth.

fig.title: Night passage between islands
lines: White light, alone in open water

q: Making your landfall at night, you time the light your plan starts from. What does it tell you?
a: A safe water mark — Morse A
o: An isolated danger — Fl(2)
A south cardinal — Q(6)+LFl
An east cardinal — Q(3)
why: Mo(A), dot-dash, is a safe water light, like Iso, Oc or LFl 10s: open water all round the mark.

fig.title: Landfall at night
lines: White light fine on the bow
A short flash, then a long one

q: Your crew notices on the chart that these two marks flash at different speeds and asks why. What do you tell them?
a: So the two can be told apart at night
o: The very quick one marks the worse danger
The very quick one is to be passed closer
The quick one is a beacon, the other a buoy
why: Neighbouring cardinals of the same kind use Q and VQ, so you can tell which one you are looking at.

q: Heading downriver to the sea at night, you see this channel light ahead. Which side do you leave it?
a: To port — you are going against the buoyage
o: To starboard — green is starboard-hand
To starboard — you are going with the buoyage
Either side — it marks mid-channel
why: Buoyage runs from seaward; heading out to sea, the starboard-hand (green) marks are left to port.

fig.note: Leaving the river for the sea · region A

q: Approaching an anchorage at night, you see a row of these lights across the bay. What are they?
a: Special marks — the chart says what they mark
o: Fishing nets — pass between them
Cardinal marks — pass to seaward
Port-hand marks — leave them to port
why: Yellow lights are special marks — a zone, a pipe, a bathing area: find on the chart what they mark.

fig.note: Across the bay ahead, at night

q: You are shading the red sector of this light onto your chart. Which water does it cover?
a: The sea between 065°T and 080°T from the light
o: The sea between 245°T and 260°T from the light
The sea between 080°T and 245°T from the light
The sea between 260°T and 065°T from the light
why: Sector limits are bearings of the light from seaward: seen from the light, the red runs out on 065°–080°.

q: You are holding the white sector of the directional light, 4 M out. How far can you stray from its centre line here before the colour changes?
a: About 1 cable either side
o: About 2 cables either side
About 3 cables either side
About ½ cable either side
why: 1 in 60: 1.5° each side at 4 M ≈ 4 × 1.5 ÷ 60 = 0.1 M, one cable; the sector narrows as you close.

fig.title: Dir Oc WRG 6s — approach
lines: You: in the white, 4.0 M out
Plan: stay well inside the white

q: Approaching the harbour on its sectored light, you see it like this, the colour never settling. What do you do?
a: Move well into the white — you are on the edge
o: Hold on — the edge is the leading line
Slow down — the light is faulty
Hold on — it is an alternating light
why: At a sector boundary the colours mix over a degree or two: the edge is uncertain — get into the middle of the white.

fig.note: Sectored light ahead · the colour won't settle

q: Entering at night on the directional light, you see it turn green. Where are you, and what do you do?
a: West of the line: come to port, then steer east of 160°
o: East of the line: come to starboard, then steer west of 160°
West of the line: come to starboard, then steer east of 160°
East of the line: come to port, then hold 160° exactly
why: Green = bearing under 158.5°T: you are west of the line, to starboard; come back to port and head up into the westerly set.

fig.title: Dir Oc WRG 6s — entering
lines: You were steering 160°T on the white
Stream sets west across the line

q: You are about to join this transit with the stream across it. What heading do you give the helm to hold the marks in line?
You are on the transit, crabbing to hold it. How long until you reach the entrance?
a: 13 min
o: 12 min
18 min
21 min
why: Along the transit you make 6.0 × cos 20° = 5.6 kn: 1.2 ÷ 5.64 = 0.21 h = 13 min.

q: A pot line round the prop stops you near a clearing line. If you lie stopped, how long until the stream carries you over it?
a: 9 min
o: 15 min
18 min
6 min
why: 0.3 M ÷ 2.0 kn = 0.15 h = 9 min — a clearing line is a limit, not a margin.

fig.title: Pot line round the prop
lines: Engine in neutral to clear it

q: Leaving the bay northward at night, you check the clearing bearing on the light astern. What do you do?
a: Alter to starboard until it reads 185°M or more
o: Alter to port until it reads 185°M or more
Hold on — under 185°M is the safe side
Alter to starboard until it reads 181°M or less
why: With the light astern, a westward drift lowers its bearing: 181°M is on the shoal side of 185°M — move east.

q: You are short-tacking north up the channel, with the church ahead as your head mark. At what hand-bearing compass reading do you tack?
why: Heading NW the church's bearing rises towards the NMT 010°T limit: 010°T − 3°E = 007°M — tack on it.

fig.title: Beating up the Steno channel
lines: Head mark: church, ahead to the north
Now on starboard tack, heading NW

q: Leaving harbour at night, you take a back bearing of the harbour light every five minutes. What is happening, and what do you do?
a: Set to port: come to starboard and aim right of 015°M
o: Set to starboard: come to port and aim left of 015°M
On track: back bearings always fall as you go
Set to port: come to port and aim left of 015°M
why: A falling back bearing puts you west of the 015° line, to port of it: get back, then steer up into the stream.

q: You are following the 5 m contour north at night, the land to port. What should the sounder read while you stay on it?
why: Depth of water = 5.0 + 2.3 = 7.3 m; the sounder reads below its transducer, 0.4 m down: 7.3 − 0.4 = 6.9 m.

fig.note: Sounder: no offset, transducer 0.4 m below waterline

q: Feeling your way towards the harbour in fog, you hear the breakwater's fog signal. How do you use it?
a: As a sign you're near, not a bearing to steer
o: Steer straight for it until it is loud
Judge your distance by how loud it is
Turn away until you can't hear it
why: Sound in fog bends and fades: a fog signal says the mark is near, never its exact bearing or range.

fig.title: Fog, approaching the harbour
lines: Heard faintly, fine on the stbd bow

q: Fog, no radar, and the stream across your approach is uncertain. How do you plan the landfall on this harbour?
a: Aim well east of it, then follow the 10 m line west
o: Aim straight at it, slowing as you near
Aim west of it, then follow the 10 m line east
Aim straight at it; turn away if it shoals
why: Aiming off tells you which side you are on when you find the contour: then turn the known way along clean water.

q: Fog closes in halfway through your pilotage between the islets, with two turns still to go. What do you do?
a: Anchor on the 6 m sand and wait for it to lift
o: Carry on, timing each leg from the plan
Follow the plotter through both turns
Turn back the way you came, at speed
why: With no radar and rocks at each turn, the safe pilotage is to stop: anchor in good holding and wait.

q: The stream has set you east of your planned track, and your crew presses 'go to' on the entrance waypoint again. What is the risk?
a: The new straight line crosses the shoal
o: None — the waypoint is in deep water
The plotter will now route round the shoal
The autopilot will steer the old track
why: 'Go to' draws a straight line from where you are now; it knows nothing of the dangers your original track avoided.

q: Creeping towards your berth at night, you glance at the plotter. Which do you steer by?
a: The compass and the marks — COG is noise here
o: The COG — it shows your real track
The average of the COG readings
The plotter's heading line, zoomed in
why: At low speed the GPS COG wanders by tens of degrees: steer by compass and by eye; COG settles only with speed.

q: Approaching at night, you see a mark on the plotter where nothing is in the water. What do you make of it?
a: A virtual AIS mark — obey it as a real one
o: A plotter fault — ignore it
A buoy off station — report it
An unlit buoy — pass close to see it
why: A virtual aid to navigation exists only as an AIS signal; it marks a real danger and is obeyed like a buoy.

fig.title: Plotter at night
lines: Nothing seen in the water there

q: You are writing leg 2 onto your pilotage card from the chart. What heading do you write?
why: True to magnetic, west is best: 247°T + 3°W = 250°M.

q: Your arrival in the bay has slipped from the afternoon to 0300. What do you change in the pilotage plan?
a: Use the directional light's white sector instead
o: Keep the transit — it will show by moonlight
Steer 312° on the compass alone
Nothing — the plotter covers the transit
why: A daylight transit vanishes at night: re-plan on lit marks — here the directional light shows the same line.

fig.title: Plan for Ormos Vathy
lines: Day plan: white chapel in line
Lights: Dir WRG 312° on the mole

q: Running west along the coast, you will turn into the bay on a bearing of the church, as your plan says. Do you turn now?
a: Not yet — hold on until it rises to 340°M
o: Yes — 330°M means the turn is past
Yes — turn now and steer 330°M for it
Not yet — wait until it is abeam to starboard
why: Running west, a mark on the starboard bow draws aft: its bearing rises from 330° towards 340° — turn when it reaches it.

q: You are on the helm for a night entry and the navigator calls "steer 047". What do you do?
a: Repeat "047" and call when steady on it
o: Steer 047 and stay quiet to keep it calm
Ask why before you turn
Turn and watch the COG reach 047
why: Closed-loop calls: the helm repeats the heading and reports when steady, so a misheard figure is caught at once.

q: Your crew, on the helm, plans to pass this green beacon 5 m off to stay in the deep channel. What do you tell them?
a: Leave it well to starboard — it stands on the rock
o: Pass it close to starboard — it marks the channel edge
Leave it to port — you are heading with the buoyage
Pass close either side — beacons stand in deep water
why: A beacon is built on the danger itself and the rocks run out round it: give it a berth, green to starboard going in.

q: Closing the coast on a clear night, you are 6 M off the harbour. What do you expect to see of its lights now?
a: Only the main light — the heads show from 3 M
o: All three, the heads a little dimmer
The heads first — they're lower and nearer
Nothing until you are within 3 M
why: The nominal range is the range in clear weather: 3M head lights won't show at 6 M — find the main light first.

fig.title: Approach to Kissamos
lines: Breakwater heads: Fl R 3s 3M, Fl G 3s 3M

q: You are approaching your planned harbour in the small hours. What do you do?
a: Anchor in the bay and enter at first light
o: Enter on the E light, keeping it close aboard
Enter with the spotlight on the W head
Enter on the plotter at dead slow
why: A narrow rocky entrance with one head unlit and town lights behind is a daylight job — and a safe anchorage is close.

fig.title: 0140, 3 M off Kaladi
lines: Entrance 50 m wide, rocks each side
Anchorage 2 M back: 8 m sand, sheltered

q: Heading in with the buoyage at night, you reach the fork. Which side of this mark do you leave to stay in the main channel?
a: To starboard — the main channel lies to port
o: To port — the main channel lies to starboard
To port — green lights are left to port at night
Either side — it marks the middle of the fork
why: In region A, Fl(2+1) G is a modified starboard-hand mark — preferred channel to port: leave it to starboard.

fig.title: Night · region A, heading in
lines: Light at the fork: Fl(2+1) G 10s
Your marina: up the main channel

q: Heading north into the bay, you follow the pilot book's directions. What do you see while you keep to them?
a: Lighthouse just left of the point — you are west of the transit
o: Lighthouse just right of the point — you are east of the transit
Lighthouse hidden behind the point — you are on the transit
Lighthouse just left of the point — you are east of the transit
why: 'Open' means not in line: with the far light showing west (left) of the near point, you are a little west of their transit.

fig.title: Pilot book — Ormos Agrilia
lines: Heading N into the bay: keep the
Ak. Mavro until the chapel is abeam
